title: Sunday SEP digest, Oct 18, 2026: AI Investor and SightBringer week in review
html:
Covers Oct 11 to Oct 18, 2026. The big story was the chip selloff: the semiconductor index (SOX) fell eight straight days, its longest losing streak since 2008, and closed Friday down 15.7% from its Oct 6 high. Both creators spent the week on the same question from opposite ends. The AI Investor says demand is sold out for years and the selloff is a discount. SightBringer says demand is real but the money to build it is getting expensive, and that is where the next problem shows up. Nothing in either feed calls for a move in the SEP.

1. The AI Investor: week in review

The short version. He stayed loudly bullish through the selloff, added to his AI infrastructure bets, and kept hedging his memory position at the same time.

His portfolio moves (paid post, Oct 15). - Opened a new position in Marvell (MRVL), a networking and custom-chip company. The full thesis article is still to come. - Added CoreWeave (CRWV) on the selloff. - Added RAM (a 2x leveraged memory fund), paid for by swapping out some Micron and DRAM-fund exposure. - Said his net exposure is now 137% (he's using leverage) and called that too high. He may scale back. - Separately, before Thursday's Taiwan earthquake he had cut half his Micron trading position and put a collar (an options hedge that caps both losses and gains) on his Micron stock. Micron reported no damage.

His memory view, updated. His Micron "memory part 6" article (Oct 13, pasted and summarized earlier) asked whether China's CXMT could end the shortage early. His answer in the Oct 15 update: high-bandwidth memory (HBM, the kind stacked next to AI chips) soaks up most new supply until 2029 or later, and CXMT is still small in HBM. Supporting data he posted: - Barclays: DDR4 contract prices up 24% in three months, with a shortage seen lasting to 2029. - Micron climbed to about 24% of DRAM revenue, one point behind SK hynix. - Apple's CEO called the memory shortage an "absolute crisis" and said Chinese suppliers are on the table. The new foldable iPhone Duo sold out with roughly 100-day lead times, and it skews toward the highest memory configurations. - CXMT swung to big profits, which he frames as proof of how large the boom is and also as the China risk he tracks.

Nvidia. He kept making the anchor case: - Jensen Huang said Nvidia now sells about $40B into each gigawatt of data center (up from about $18B) and takes roughly 40% of big-cloud AI spending and about 80% outside the big clouds. - BofA says Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron trade around 13x forward earnings, the same range as Cisco after the dot-com crash, even though there's been no crash. That only holds if earnings estimates hold. - His Saturday line: at Apple's valuation Nvidia would be about $550 a share, at Tesla's about $3,000. - Smaller items: Meta adopting Nvidia networking for its biggest AI data centers, Mercedes calling Nvidia its most important self-driving partner, and Nvidia compute on SpaceX satellites ("Star Mind"), with Jensen calling it the "perfect payload."

Demand signals he leaned on. AWS is reportedly sold out "beyond 2028." AMD's Lisa Su said agent traffic is up 14x this year. ASML says even ~30% capacity increases in 2027 and 2028 won't meet AI chip demand, with customers already ordering for 2029 to 2030.

Where he admits risk. - Power. His main constraint is how fast new power comes online. - Gigawatt forecasts. He thinks consensus estimates for new data-center gigawatts are too high versus his own project tracker. Early Sunday he suggested an outside research firm had been too bullish on gigawatts added per year. - Financing. CoreWeave fell about 25% on the week and its 2032 bonds yield above 15%. He defends the model (contracts signed first, debt raised against them) and pushed back hard on critics. Anthropic is offering a coupon above 10% on a $60B chip-financing package, and its IPO talk dropped from about $2T to about $1.5T.

2. SightBringer: week in review

The short version. Two paid forecasts (S&P 500 and silver), one paid Strive (ASST) forecast announced, and a steady stream of essays on AI, ownership, and the dollar. His X account has been quiet since Friday afternoon, with no new paid posts announced.

S&P 500 forecast (Oct 14, pasted and summarized Oct 15). This is the one that matters most for the plan. - Year-end 2026: base case 50% for 7,600 to 8,200 (center about 7,900). Downside 31% below 7,600 (center about 7,200, with a 5% severe case near 6,500). Upside 19% above 8,200. - That's a real shift from the version in our plan, which had the base at 62% and the bear case at 12%. Downside odds more than doubled. - 2027 year-end center about 8,500, with a 57% "recovery" case above 8,400. - His thesis: the earnings engine is intact, but financing for AI infrastructure is now the constraint. The chain he's watching is credit stress, then hyperscaler capex, then forward earnings estimates. - He'd turn more bullish if earnings estimates keep rising, AI cash flow catches up, real 10-year yields fall to 2.5% or below, AI credit stabilizes, and breadth improves. He'd turn more bearish on falling estimates, stress reaching hyperscaler capex, or real yields at 3% or higher with weak growth. Real yields were about 2.9% when he wrote it.

Silver forecast (Oct 13). Full text still not on file. The preview says silver is around $60, back where it was in June, while gold holds above $4,000 under the same pressure (the Fed hiking again, real yields near 3%, a stronger dollar). He calls that divergence the key clue. The revised targets are behind the paywall. The SEP holds no silver, so this is context only.

Strive (ASST) forecast (Oct 11). First full Inner Ring forecast on Strive. The public teaser says Strive holds about 29,000 to 30,000 BTC with rising BTC per share, but faces oil above $100, yields above 5%, and common stock trading above the value of its bitcoin. The full map isn't on file.

The essays, grouped by theme. - AI economics. The $10T US AI buildout is a "prisoner's dilemma": every hyperscaler builds because rivals do, which risks excess capacity, and cheaper intelligence squeezes revenue against depreciation and power costs. Value may shift from whoever finances compute to whoever uses it. Railroads and telecom changed the world and still wiped out their original investors. - What stays scarce. AI makes expertise cheap to copy, so knowledge moats erode, including for AI companies over time. What stays scarce: energy, computing infrastructure, physical production, capital, distribution. "The biggest fortunes go to whoever controls the bottlenecks intelligence can't remove." - Software. Software's hidden asset was customers' inability to leave. Agents that can migrate data and rebuild tools give customers an exit, and "margins can fall before revenues do." He flagged Microsoft 365 seat economics as exposed, though Microsoft is protected by identity, data and compliance. The scarce skill ahead is governing and verifying agents. - Market breadth. The S&P was within 1% of a record while 206 of its companies were down more than 30%. An index carried by a few giants is very sensitive to a letdown from those giants. - Money and debt. Debt is being inflated away the 1946 to 1975 way, with nominal growth (~8.5%) running above the average Treasury rate (~3.5%). A gold revaluation would be a headline, not a fix. Stablecoins are a real but small buyer of Treasury bills (under 4%). Watch the Nov 4 Treasury refunding. - AI agents and banks. If millions of depositors have agents watching yields and risk, they can all move at once, so a solvent bank can go illiquid with no rumor needed. - Ownership versus wages. A recurring theme: AI pushes the gains to owners of compute, IP and equity, while the old path from wages to ownership weakens. Owning productive assets is the point of a growth account like the SEP. - Plus non-market posts (alignment, consciousness, aphorisms) that don't bear on the plan.

3. How this relates to the SEP plan

What the week confirmed

  • Memory is still structural. Barclays' shortage-to-2029 call, Apple's "crisis" comment, and the AI Investor's view that HBM absorbs new supply until 2029 or later all back the DRAM position. SightBringer said nothing new on Micron this week, but his "bottlenecks intelligence can't remove" frame puts memory on the scarce side.
  • Nvidia as the anchor. Both men's frameworks still point here. The AI Investor sees rising revenue per gigawatt and a growing share of spending. SightBringer's "own the bottlenecks" argument covers computing infrastructure. Neither sees anything broken at Nvidia.
  • Governance layer over seat-based software. SightBringer's switching-cost and "govern the agents" essays fit the plan's split: NOW and PANW are the governance names, and seat-based software is what gets compressed.
  • SpaceX. Star Mind (Nvidia racks on SpaceX satellites, volume production next year per Elon) and Jensen's "perfect payload" comment support the reason SPCX is in the account. Elon's "$100T in under 10 years" claim is Elon talking, not analysis.
  • Amazon and Google. AWS sold out past 2028, Google's 3.6 GW nuclear power deal, and Anthropic's $125B Google TPU lease all support the AMZN and GOOGL positions.

What the week challenged

  • Timing. The plan was executed Oct 7, the day after the chip index's Oct 6 peak, so the new DRAM position was bought right before the 15.7% drop. The plan sized memory as a starter position, without leverage, because of exactly this risk. This is the "never have the year that sets you back five" scenario SightBringer posted about, and Hunter's call to skip 2x funds looks better after this week.
  • The S&P map moved. The plan's macro backdrop assumed a 62% base case near 8,000. SightBringer now has a 50% base near 7,900 and 31% odds of finishing the year below 7,600. That's not a call to do anything, but the backdrop is less friendly than when the plan was written.
  • Concentration. NVDA is about a third of the account. SightBringer's breadth warning (a market leaning on a few giants is fragile to their earnings) applies directly to that kind of concentration. The plan accepts that on purpose; it's worth knowing when the next tests come (see the watch list).

Where they agree and disagree

They agree demand is real and physical bottlenecks (chips, memory, power, equipment) are the scarce assets. They both name power as the constraint. They both see financing as where the stress shows up.

The disagreement is what the financing stress means: - The AI Investor reads high CoreWeave bond yields and Anthropic's 10%+ coupon as noise. The contracts are signed, demand is sold out, and the selloff is a gift. He's buying. - SightBringer reads the same data as the transmission belt: credit stress, then capex cuts, then earnings estimate cuts. His prisoner's-dilemma essay goes further, saying overbuilding plus falling token prices could hurt whoever owns the most depreciating hardware. That's a direct challenge to neocloud bets like CoreWeave. - For the SEP: the plan owns no CoreWeave, so the most exposed name isn't in the account. Nvidia sits upstream (it sells the hardware), which both frameworks favor over the renters. The open question is whether stress at the renters eventually reaches Nvidia's orders. SightBringer's checkpoints are built to answer that.

One smaller tension worth noting. Jensen says token costs fall 30 to 40 times a year. The AI Investor treats that as a demand engine (cheap tokens beat expensive labor). SightBringer treats it as margin compression for whoever sells intelligence. Both can be true at once. It's good for chip volume and bad for pricing power at the model layer.

Updates to the plan's live tensions

  1. MSTR torque. No new MSTR or STRC data this week. The Oct 28 shareholder vote is 10 days out. The new ASST forecast flags a premium to BTC-backed value and rate headwinds, but the full map isn't on file. MSTR and ASST stay untouched as deliberate amplifiers.
  2. Memory 2027. This one moved. The AI Investor's earlier worry about a 2027 HBM oversupply looks softer now that he says HBM absorbs supply until 2029 or later. But he's hedging his own Micron stock with a collar and trimmed his trading position, so his words are more bullish than his positioning. SightBringer's 25% "digestion" scenario ("right company, wrong multiple") is close to what Micron's price did this week (down 12.5%) while the fundamentals held up. The starter-sized, unleveraged DRAM position still fits both.
  3. Quantum hedge. Nothing new from either. QTUM, WQTM and QBTS stay as deliberate insurance.

Dated watch items (updated)

  • Oct 21: Meta earnings, SightBringer's first S&P checkpoint and a read on AI capex.
  • Oct 28: MSTR shareholder vote, Microsoft and Google earnings, and the FOMC meeting. For Microsoft, watch for any sign of the seat-pricing pressure SightBringer describes.
  • Nov 2: Apple earnings (iPhone Duo demand and memory costs).
  • Nov 4: Treasury refunding (SightBringer flagged it twice) and Coherent earnings (optical networking).
  • November: Anthropic's share sale at about $1.5T, a gauge of how the market is pricing private AI.
  • Nov 30: does STRC hold par?
  • Dec 9: FOMC.
  • Q1 2027: MSTR external STRC issuance, SightBringer's "decisive test."
  • Ongoing: real 10-year yield versus SightBringer's 3% downgrade line (about 2.9% at last read). CoreWeave bond yields as the stress gauge both men are watching. BTC's $83K to $86K warning zone and Micron versus the AI Investor's $1,200 caution zone (neither was updated in this week's posts). The CLARITY Act had no news this week.

Still waiting on pastes

  • SightBringer's Silver 2026 to 2027 Forecast Update (Oct 13): post link.
  • If you want the Strive (ASST) map in the plan: Strive forecast.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice. SEP IRA only.

title: AI Investor Quips, Oct 15: Micron after the Taiwan earthquake, and a TSMC earnings preview
html:
• MU trade updates (two Quips). A 4.8-magnitude earthquake hit Taiwan Thursday morning. Micron said its Taiwan factory is fine and it's doing a 100% machine inspection before resuming, with no supply disruption found so far. He said this backs up his earlier de-risking: before the quake he had cut half his Micron trading position and fully protected his Micron stock with a collar (an options hedge that caps both the downside and the upside).
  • TSMC earnings preview. TSMC was due to report Oct 16 before the open. He said to watch for proof the AI data-center buildout is still speeding up. The expectations he cited were about $34.08B in revenue, about a 59.3% gross margin, and an update on its advanced-packaging (CoWoS) capacity ramp. He sees TSMC as a direct read on AI spending, and strong results should lift the memory chain (SK hynix, Micron, Sandisk).

SEP touch (light): The quake was a reminder of the Taiwan risk he always flags, and nothing broke. The TSMC read-through matters for the SEP's DRAM position. His hedging uses options, which are on hold for the SEP, so it's context only.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

title: AI Investor on X, Oct 16 midday to Oct 17 early morning: chip selloff, Jensen backs CoreWeave, Apple calls memory a "crisis"
html:
Big picture: Chip stocks had a rough week (SOXX down about 10% after eight straight down days; Micron off 12.5%, Broadcom 7.1%, Nvidia 5.4% for the week). His posts push back on the fear: demand is sold out for years, memory prices are still rising, and he says he's buying the dip.

  • 12:23 PM, Jensen backs CoreWeave. Jensen Huang told Bloomberg CoreWeave's strength is "improving every day" and it doesn't need an Nvidia bailout. Context: CRWV fell 15.5% Wednesday, then swung from $59.51 to close at $69.69 Thursday. Its credit insurance prices hit a record and its 2032 bonds yield above 15%, so the bond market is clearly nervous. Nvidia owns about 10%. Cantor (target $176) and BofA (target $140) both stayed bullish. https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111130889308840391
  • 2:20 AM, David Sacks on CoreWeave. Sacks argues the CoreWeave selloff is market volatility, not a collapse in demand, and that what matters for its debt is how creditworthy its long-term contract customers are (big names like Microsoft). https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111341598693003398
  • 4:52 PM, BofA: chip stocks already priced like post-crash Cisco (his most-viewed post, ~86k views). BofA's Vivek Arya says Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron trade at about 13x forward earnings on average, the same range Cisco sat in after the dot-com crash, even though this cycle hasn't crashed. The catch is that this only holds if earnings estimates hold. His take: with DRAM contract prices expected up 10–15% and NAND up 15–20% in Q4, the "crash" multiple may just be a discount on growth. https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111198700840308777
  • 8:42 PM, Apple CEO calls the memory shortage an "absolute crisis." Apple's CEO John Ternus told TIME every supply option is on the table, including Chinese memory makers CXMT and YMTC (both on a US defense blacklist). Micron lobbied against that, and senators are pushing back. 12:28 AM follow-up: the new foldable iPhone Duo sold out in minutes with new orders slipping into 2027, which is great for Apple revenue but adds even more pressure on memory supply. https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111256570801824074
  • 2:38 AM, China's CXMT swings to big profits. CXMT's Q3 revenue rose roughly 6x year over year, and it flipped from a loss to a large profit for the first nine months. He frames this as a sign of how big the AI memory boom is (JPMorgan sees the HBM market going from $64B in 2026 to $280B in 2028), not a one-off. It's also the China supply risk he's been tracking for Micron. https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111346194840748502
  • 1:55 AM, Amazon's AI compute is sold out past 2028. Ben Horowitz says Andy Jassy told him AWS is sold out "beyond 2028," which he calls fundamentally different from the dot-com bubble, when demand didn't exist yet. AI Investor: the demand problem "is only in the imagination of some random bears on X." https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111335225183838580
  • 11:38 PM, Anthropic's $60B chip-financing deal. Anthropic is offering Blackstone a coupon above 10% to anchor the riskier tier of a $60B debt package arranged by Broadcom, which pays for its five-year Google TPU lease ($125B committed, 3.5 GW starting 2027). It would be the largest chip financing ever. The high interest rate shows how expensive AI-buildout money is getting. https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111300877944492390
  • 4:55 PM, ASML may build a hybrid bonding tool. SemiAnalysis read ASML patents and thinks it's developing a tool for hybrid bonding, the chip-stacking step used to build HBM memory. Besi, the current specialist, fell 3%. https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111199313611432257
  • 12:27 PM, Jensen on Lex Fridman: "we've achieved AGI" by Lex's definition (an AI that could start and run a billion-dollar company), but he puts the odds of AI agents building something like Nvidia at zero. https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111132002514788518
  • 2:46 AM, Jensen on SpaceX: Nvidia compute is the "perfect payload" for orbit because it's the highest-value computing per watt and always has renters. Ties to the Star Mind satellite program. https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111348141694001206
  • 3:05 AM, buying the dip. "When the market is selling off great stocks, you know what a fundamentals-driven investor like me is doing." (Links out; likely a Patreon promo.) https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2111352886710222999

SEP touch (light): This week's drop hit the exact names in the SEP's core (NVDA anchor, DRAM). Everything he posted argues the fundamentals haven't changed: compute sold out past 2028, memory prices still rising, Apple calling the shortage a crisis. The real risk he's watching is financing stress at CoreWeave and similar companies, and the SEP doesn't own CRWV. Nothing here calls for a move. A selloff is the "don't chase, don't panic" test the plan was built for.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

title: AI Investor on X, Oct 15 night to Oct 16 morning: Jensen on Nvidia's growing slice of AI spending, Anthropic's IPO valuation cut, Star Mind math
html:
• 3:42 AM, Jensen Huang on the BG2 podcast. Nvidia went from a GPU company, to the biggest networking company, to now becoming one of the largest CPU companies ("surely the fastest growing one"). What Nvidia sells into each gigawatt of data center went from about $18B to about $20B to now $40B+, and Jensen expects it to keep rising. Nvidia's share of world AI capex went from single digits six years ago to about 40% at the big cloud companies and about 80% outside them (on-prem and neoclouds), with both halves doubling every year. https://x.com/The_AI_Investor/status/2110999766712869351
  • 1:43 AM, overnight news roundup. (1) Anthropic: Reuters says IPO investors are now talking about a ~$1.5T valuation for its November share sale, down from ~$2T. Q3 revenue rose 45% to $16.8B (from $11.6B in Q2) and was profitable on an adjusted basis, but growth is slowing after Q2 more than doubled. html:
Source: @The_Prophet_ (posts from about 12:19 to 3:16 PM ET)

The S&P 500 is a story of concentration, not broad prosperity (~1:06 PM ET)

He quotes a Kobeissi Letter stat: the S&P 500 is within 1% of a record high while 206 of its companies are down more than 30%. His point is that the index is weighted by company size, so a small group of giants with strong earnings, strong balance sheets, and AI infrastructure exposure can carry it to new highs while hundreds of other companies are in their own bear market. Investors are moving money toward the businesses that control the next generation of productive capacity and away from those whose work AI can copy. The risk he flags is that an index leaning on a few names is very sensitive to any earnings letdown from those names, and that weak breadth (most stocks lagging) shows stress the headline number hides. His closing line: the danger is mistaking the index's strength for the strength of the whole economy.

AI breaks the link between inventing something and owning its value (~12:50 PM ET)

Quoting a viral "there are no moats left" post. Expertise used to be protected because it was hard and expensive to copy. AI makes it cheap to rebuild what took years, so intellectual property and know-how lose pricing power and margins get squeezed, and that includes AI companies themselves over time. What stays scarce is energy, computing infrastructure, physical production, capital, distribution, and control of real-world systems. His line: the biggest fortunes of the AI age go to whoever controls the bottlenecks intelligence can't remove.

The professional middle class is being repriced (~12:44 PM ET)

Quoting a stat on entry-level hiring declines in AI-exposed fields (design/media/writing down about 41%, customer support about 34%, clerical about 31%, finance about 23%). The old deal of getting skills and credentials, entering a profession, and building wealth worked because skilled thinking work was scarce. As AI makes that work abundant, companies lose the reason to train junior people, and the rewards shift to whoever owns the infrastructure. He expects the economy to keep producing wealth with fewer people needed to produce it.

"Just predicting tokens" misunderstands intelligence (~12:56 PM ET)

A reply to the claim that AI models don't "understand" anything. No single brain cell understands math either; understanding emerges from how the parts are organized. Training a model to predict language forces it to build working models of physics, cause and effect, and human intent, so prediction at scale becomes a route to real general capability, even if it's imperfect.

Short posts

  • Humanity may be the first species to understand the universe, but it won't stay the only intelligence that can.
  • "He who controls the spice controls the universe," a Dune line quoted back at a reader who said Frank Herbert predicted all this in 1965.
  • A repost of his Oct 14 note that the updated S&P 500 2026 forecast and first 2027 outlook are live for Inner Ring subscribers. That's the same paid post already flagged, not a new release.

SEP touch

This is consistent with the existing thesis of owning scarce productive assets and infrastructure over businesses built on copyable knowledge. The breadth point is a reminder that a heavily concentrated index can stall if a few leaders disappoint. There's no new ticker call and no forecast change. Deeper plan work waits for Sunday.

Educational analysis, not professional financial advice.

Summary

Software’s hidden asset was the customer’s inability to leave — integrations, historical data, customized workflows, trained staff — which underwrote recurring revenue and valuations. AI agents that can rebuild functionality, migrate records, recreate integrations, and test replacements give customers a credible exit. Even without leaving, that option weakens renewals, shortens contracts, and compresses feature premiums: margins can fall before revenues do (his strongest early signal). Deepest inversion: software made itself indispensable; AI may make customers independent of software vendors. Market still prices many names as if customers have nowhere else to go. title: SightBringer — X — Wage inflation vs ownership / AI fracture
html:
• Source: https://x.com/The_Prophet_/status/2109494561664094516
  • Posted: 2026-10-12 ~12:01 AM ET
  • Type: public X (long note; quotes $100k→~$195k purchasing-power chart)

Summary

A $100k salary in 2000 needs ~$195k today for the same purchasing power — but the bigger fracture is the deteriorating bargain: work → save → acquire assets → independence. Assets (stocks/businesses/property) are claims on future production that compound; wages must be continually earned, and rising asset prices force workers to sell more time to buy ownership. A $200k earner with no wealth can be more vulnerable than a $90k earner with a paid-off home and investments. AI amplifies this: trillions into systems that cheapen intelligence/labor so owners capture more output while wages that fund ownership face pressure. “The mechanism that allowed labor to become capital is weakening precisely as capital becomes less dependent on labor.” Prize was never the six-figure salary — it was freedom from needing one. Feedback loop: government needs private buyers for debt at affordable yields; the same system uses that debt as collateral. Rising yields raise financing costs, hurt bond books, shrink warehouse capacity, and force more issuance for interest — undermining absorption. Political path of least resistance is making gov debt easier to hold (bills, regs, stablecoin reserves, backstops, possible renewed CB buys) rather than tax hikes or spending cuts. Financial repression can start before announced QE; QE that swaps fixed for floating-rate exposure can leave fiscal arithmetic unresolved while staking dollar purchasing-power credibility.
